passage: Last winter my flatmate Afreen got the worst flu I've ever seen. I'm Amandeep, and I'm not a natural nurse; I panic at the sight of blood. But I did what my mother used to do for us: a jug of water by the bed, curtains half closed, a check-in every couple of hours. Afreen was a monster. She said I breathed too loudly, threw a pillow at me when I brought khichdi, and cried because her phone charger was "looking at her". I laughed that one off. On the third night she seemed muddled about what day it was, and her breathing sounded fast. That frightened me more than any pillow. I rang the doctor's night line, they told us to come in, and I took her in a cab. She was fine after a few days. She still apologises for the pillow. I tell her sick people get a free pass on grumpy.

qa.q: What did Afreen throw at Amandeep?
qa.a: A pillow.

qa.q: What made Amandeep feel frightened on the third night?
qa.a: Amandeep felt scared when Afreen seemed muddled about the day and her breathing sounded fast, far more than by any grumpiness.

qa.a: Keeping water, rest and check-ins going, shrugging off the grumpiness, and ringing the doctor's line at once when danger signs appeared.

qa.a: She seems embarrassed and grateful, still apologising for the pillow.

grounding: Shows a caregiver keeping fluids and rest in view, not taking a sick friend's grumpiness personally, and calling a doctor when danger signs appear.

passage:
Warden's log, Saturday night
Most of D-block went home for the weekend, but Jomon stayed back to look after his roommate Karthik, who has had a fever since Thursday. I looked in three times today. Each time Jomon had water and a bowl of rice gruel ready, the fan on low, and a notebook where he had written when Karthik last drank and slept. Karthik was short with him, told him to stop hovering, and at one point said he wanted his mother, not Jomon. Jomon just said, "Fair," and carried on. At eight Jomon came to my office: Karthik was getting harder to wake. We called the campus doctor, who came at once and arranged a hospital check. Jomon went with him. I phoned Karthik's parents tonight, and I'll make sure Jomon gets some rest tomorrow too.

qa.q: What did Jomon write in his notebook?
qa.a: When Karthik last drank and slept.

qa.q: How did Jomon take Karthik saying he wanted his mother, not Jomon?
qa.a: Jomon seemed unoffended and steady, taking the grumpiness as the illness rather than an insult, and simply said "Fair".

qa.q: What was the most important thing Jomon did at eight?
qa.a: He noticed a danger sign, Karthik getting harder to wake, and went straight to the warden so the doctor came at once.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents feel on getting the call?
qa.a: Worried, but likely grateful that their son had someone watching closely and acting quickly.

grounding: Shows a caregiver keeping fluids, rest and notes, accepting a sick friend's grumpiness, and getting a doctor at once when a danger sign appears.

passage: When Ujjwal read aloud in Class 6, his voice cracked in the middle of "photosynthesis", squeaky then deep. Dhruv snorted, and half the class laughed. At home in their Indore flat, Ujjwal slammed his bag down, refused dinner, and shut himself in the bathroom, where he noticed again the new smell under his arms and the dark fuzz on his lip. His body felt like someone else's. Papa knocked. "Ujju, can I come in? I remember this." He sat on the edge of the tub and explained simply: voices crack while they deepen, sweat changes, hair grows, and it happens to everyone in their own time. "Nothing's wrong with you. It's puberty. We'll get you a deodorant tomorrow." Ujjwal came out and ate two rotis.

qa.a: Photosynthesis.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when he shut himself in the bathroom?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, as if his changing body belonged to someone else.

qa.q: Why did Papa's explanation help?
qa.a: It was honest and simple, told Ujjwal nothing was wrong, and offered a practical step, which eased his shame.

grounding: Shows a child in early puberty feeling embarrassed and moody as his body changes, and an honest, simple explanation reducing the shame.

passage: Last year, when I was ten, my body started changing before my friends' did. My chest felt sore and looked different, and I began hunching over in PE so nobody would notice. I snapped at everyone and cried over small things. I thought something was wrong with me. Then Farida Aunty, my mother's friend who is a nurse, came to stay. She noticed the hunching and asked me gently. She showed me pictures in a book and explained that it was puberty, that it starts at different times for everyone, and that it's normal. She took me to buy soft vests. I still felt shy. But I stopped hunching, and I stopped thinking I was broken. I'm Aparna, and now I tell my younger cousin the truth when she asks.

qa.q: What did Farida Aunty take Aparna to buy?
qa.a: Soft vests.

qa.q: How might Aparna's friends have seen the hunching and snapping?
qa.a: They may have thought Aparna was just grumpy, not knowing about the worry underneath.

grounding: Shows a child whose body starts changing early feeling embarrassed and self-conscious, and a simple, honest explanation reducing shame.

passage: I'm Jyoti, Ayesha's older sibling, and last Sunday I watched Ammi do something nobody did for me. Ayesha is ten. After lunch Ammi sat her on the divan with a book and a packet of sanitary pads and talked plainly, the way she talks about recipes: what periods are, why they happen, what to do if one starts at school. When Ayesha giggled, Ammi didn't hush her. She waited, then carried on. When Ayesha asked if it hurts, Ammi said, "Sometimes a little. Tell me, and we'll handle it." I couldn't tell exactly what Ayesha felt. She went a bit red. But afterwards she tucked a pad into the inside pocket of her school bag, carefully, like a secret key. I learned from a rumour in Class 7. She won't have to.

qa.a: Into the inside pocket of her school bag.

qa.q: What might Ayesha's red face and careful tucking of the pad suggest?

qa.q: What made Ammi's explanation work?
qa.a: She spoke early and plainly, didn't giggle or hush, answered the question about pain honestly, and gave a plan for school.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ammi's talk, compared with Jyoti's own experience?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as a gift, since Jyoti learned from a rumour in Class 7 and Ayesha now won't have to.

passage: Kiran, you asked why I'm not shy about these things. When I was eleven, in Jabalpur, nobody told me anything. When my period came, I thought I was dying. passage: Sabina saw the screenshot at 6:10 pm: her private message about her crush, forwarded by Gopika to the class group. Her face burned. In their Hyderabad flat she typed fast: "You're a snake. At 7:15 she opened the drawer. The feeling was still there, but smaller. She deleted the draft and wrote instead: "That was private. I'm really hurt. Please delete it and tell me why." passage: When I was fourteen, my feelings came like monsoon storms: sudden, huge, gone an hour later. I'm Hafsa, and I once slammed my bedroom door so hard the latch broke, after Abbu said no to a school trip. I once sent Payal a message saying I never wanted to see her again, over a seat on the bus, and spent a week trying to fix it. What helped wasn't anyone telling me to calm down. It was noticing the pattern. My cousin said, "The feeling is real, but it isn't permanent." So I made myself a deal: when the storm comes, I wait one hour. I walk three rounds of the colony park with loud music, or I write it out in the back of my maths notebook, or I call Payal and just rant. Most of the time, after an hour, I don't want to send the message anymore. There are a lot fewer broken latches now.

qa.q: What broke when Hafsa slammed the door?
qa.a: The latch.

qa.a: Hafsa felt regretful, spending a week trying to fix it.
